items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.

items.title: pH 1 is ten times more acidic than pH 2 — and a hundred times more than pH 3
items.claim: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 — looks linear. It's not. pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen-ion concentration. Each unit is a factor of ten.
items.prompt: How many times more H+ does stomach acid (pH 1) have than pure water (pH 7)?
items.reveal:
pH = -log10[H+]. Stomach acid at pH 1 has [H+] = 0.1 M. Pure water at pH 7 has [H+] = 10 to the minus 7 M. The ratio is 10 to the 6 — a million.

This is why diluting a strong acid even tenfold barely changes its pH — the absolute concentration drops by a factor of 10, but pH only shifts by 1 unit.

The same applies to the Richter scale (earthquakes), decibels (sound), and stellar magnitudes (brightness). Logarithmic scales let humans handle quantities spanning many orders of magnitude — but they hide the underlying spread.
items.why: Linear-looking scales can describe quantities ranging over 14 orders of magnitude. The arithmetic of acidity must respect the log.

items.title: You can buy crystals of a 'noble gas' compound by the gram
items.claim: Xenon difluoride (XeF2) is sold by chemical suppliers. Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4) was first synthesised in 1962 by Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne National Lab. The textbook claim that noble gases 'do not react' was overturned 60 years ago.
items.prompt: What made xenon chemistry possible in 1962?

options.text: Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed xenon's first ionisation energy (1170 kJ/mol) is almost identical to O2's (1175 kJ/mol). Since PtF6 oxidised O2, he tried Xe + PtF6 — and got XePtF6, the first noble gas compound
Lasers were finally powerful enough to break Xe bonds

items.reveal:
In early 1962 Bartlett had been making PtF6 — a brilliant red solid — and noticed a sample turned red on contact with air. Analysis showed O2+ PtF6-: PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2.

Bartlett looked up xenon's first ionisation energy and saw the near-equality with O2. He reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise Xe. The synthesis of yellow XePtF6 made the front page of Chemical & Engineering News.

Within months Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating Xe and F2 in a nickel container at 400°C. Today there are dozens of xenon compounds (XeO3, XeO4, XeF6, KrF2, ArF — the last only at cryogenic temperatures).

Helium and neon remain genuinely unreactive in normal conditions — their ionisation energies (2080 and 2370 kJ/mol) are too high for any known oxidiser to defeat.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.
